# Energy and Its Units — 1.2 Units of Energy

::: concept T-joule
term: Joule
definition: [p.3: "The SI unit of energy is the joule (J)."]
plain: The joule is the standard (SI) unit of energy; it is small, so chemists often use kilojoules, where 1 kJ is 1000 J. [p.3: "A joule is a small amount of energy, so chemists often report energies in kilojoules (kJ); 1 kJ = 1000 J."]
example: One joule is the kinetic energy of a 2 kg object moving at 1 meter per second. [p.3: "One joule is the kinetic energy of a 2-kg object moving at a speed of 1 meter per second."]
:::

::: concept T-calorie
term: Calorie
definition: [p.3: "An older unit, the calorie (cal), was originally defined as the amount of energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 gram of water by 1 degree Celsius."]
plain: The calorie is an older energy unit; today it is defined as exactly 4.184 joules. [p.3: "Today the calorie is defined in terms of the joule:"] [p.3: "1 cal = 4.184 J (exactly)"]
misconception: Wrong: the Calorie on a food label is the same as a calorie. | Right: a food Calorie (capital C) is a kilocalorie, which is 1000 calories. [p.4: "The Calorie (with a capital C) that appears on food labels is actually a kilocalorie: 1 Calorie = 1 kcal = 1000 cal."]
:::

::: formula EQ-1.2
name: Converting between calories and joules
latex: 1\,\text{cal} = 4.184\,\text{J}
where: cal = calorie; J = joule. [p.3: "An older unit, the calorie (cal), was originally defined"] [p.3: "The SI unit of energy is the joule (J)."]
holds-when: Always, exactly: the calorie is defined in terms of the joule. [p.3: "1 cal = 4.184 J (exactly)"]
source: [p.3: "1 cal = 4.184 J (exactly)"]
check: J = cal * 4.184
rearrange: cal = J / 4.184
:::

::: worked-example WE-1.2
title: Converting Calories to Joules
source: Example 1.2 [p.4: "A snack releases 250 cal of energy when it is burned."]
problem: How many joules does a snack release if it releases 250 cal? [p.4: "A snack releases 250 cal of energy when it is burned. How many joules is this?"]
step: Use the conversion factor from Equation 1.2: 1 cal = 4.184 J.
step: Multiply: 250 cal × 4.184 J/cal = 1046 J.
step: Convert to kilojoules: 1046 J is about 1.05 kJ.
calc: E = 250[cal] => 1046[J]
calc: E => 1.05[kJ]
result: The snack releases 1046 J, or about 1.05 kJ. [p.4: "250 cal × 4.184 J/cal = 1046 J, or about 1.05 kJ."]
:::

::: question Q-1.2-01
type: mcq
bloom: understand
ask: Why do chemists often report energies in kilojoules rather than joules?
option A: A joule is a small amount of energy.
option B: The joule is not an SI unit.
option C: Food labels are required to use kilojoules.
option D: A kilojoule is smaller than a joule.
answer: A
why: The book says the joule is small, which is why kilojoules are common. [p.3: "A joule is a small amount of energy, so chemists often report energies in kilojoules (kJ)"]
why-not B: The joule is the SI unit of energy. [p.3: "The SI unit of energy is the joule (J)."]
why-not C: Food labels use the Calorie, which is a kilocalorie. [p.4: "The Calorie (with a capital C) that appears on food labels is actually a kilocalorie"]
why-not D: A kilojoule is 1000 joules, so it is larger. [p.3: "so chemists often report energies in kilojoules (kJ); 1 kJ = 1000 J"]
covers: LO-1.2-1, T-joule
:::

::: question Q-1.2-02
type: numeric
bloom: apply
ask: How many joules are in 75.0 cal?
calc: E = 75.0[cal] => 313.8[J]
answer: 314[J]
why: Multiply by the exact conversion factor, 4.184 J per calorie. [p.3: "1 cal = 4.184 J (exactly)"]
covers: LO-1.2-2, EQ-1.2
:::

::: question Q-1.2-03
type: cloze
bloom: remember
ask: The SI unit of energy is the ____.
answer: joule
accept: joule (J)
why: The book names the joule as the SI unit of energy. [p.3: "The SI unit of energy is the joule (J)."]
covers: LO-1.2-1, T-joule
:::

::: question Q-1.2-04
type: tf
bloom: understand
ask: A food Calorie (with a capital C) equals 1000 calories.
answer: true
why: A food Calorie is a kilocalorie, which is 1000 cal. [p.4: "1 Calorie = 1 kcal = 1000 cal."]
covers: LO-1.2-2, T-calorie
:::
